DMCR QuickStart Walkthrough

DMCR QuickStart Walkthrough

13 numbered steps, two DBAs at the same time. anika.rao and leo.martin each run their own DMCR Web on their own clone of one repository. One release with two projects: A · Items (a table and two rows, DDL and DML) and B · Pricing (a function). Both DBAs change the same function; a deploy is refused until anika merges the two with a merge change, then marks project A never send to prod: the release goes to test with A and B, and to prod with B only. For each step: what to click and type, the SQL to paste and what you should see; under it the real DMCR Web screen, captured while these exact steps were run. The SQL never names a schema; test is qs_test (schema zp_st), prod is qs_prod (schema zp).

Something looks different on your screen? Tell me the step number and what you saw, for example #12: 001 is on the prod list.

Set up the test and prod databases

For a PC with PostgreSQL installed and DBeaver connected as the postgres user. These run in DBeaver, once. Auto-commit must be on in the SQL editor, because CREATE DATABASE cannot run in a transaction.

NameWhat it isPasswordWho uses it
postgresThe server's superuserAlready set when PostgreSQL was installed: the one DBeaver usesYou, only for these steps
zp_dbo_st / zp_dboThe database admin user on test / prod. It owns the database and a schema of the same name, with full accessYou set it in step 1DMCR: type it into the first-run wizard, and it is kept in the OS keychain, not in dmcr.cfg
zp_st / zpThe role on test / prod that the admin user grants access to, with GRANT SELECT ... TO ${app_role}None: it cannot log inYour application's users, through step 5

1. Connected to the postgres database

Under your connection, right-click the postgres database, choose SQL Editor > New SQL script, paste this and run it with Alt+X (Execute SQL Script). Use your own two passwords, and keep them for step 6. On two separate servers, run the test lines on the test server and the prod lines on the prod server.

-- test
CREATE ROLE zp_dbo_st LOGIN PASSWORD 'choose_a_password';
CREATE ROLE zp_st;
CREATE DATABASE qs_test OWNER zp_dbo_st;

-- prod
CREATE ROLE zp_dbo LOGIN PASSWORD 'choose_another_password';
CREATE ROLE zp;
CREATE DATABASE qs_prod OWNER zp_dbo;

Check the admin users:

SELECT rolname, rolcanlogin, rolsuper
FROM pg_roles
WHERE rolname IN ('zp_dbo_st', 'zp_dbo');

You should see both with rolcanlogin = true and rolsuper = false. They are not superusers: their full access comes from owning the database and the schema.

2. Connected to qs_test

CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS zp_dbo_st AUTHORIZATION zp_dbo_st;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA zp_dbo_st TO zp_st;

No qs_test in DBeaver's list? Refresh it, or make a new connection with Database set to qs_test.

3. Connected to qs_prod

CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS zp_dbo AUTHORIZATION zp_dbo;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA zp_dbo TO zp;

4. On each one, check it

SELECT current_database(), nspname, nspowner::regrole
FROM pg_namespace
WHERE nspname IN ('zp_dbo_st', 'zp_dbo');

You should see qs_test | zp_dbo_st | zp_dbo_st and qs_prod | zp_dbo | zp_dbo.

5. Only for your application's users

DMCR does not need this. A login gets what the role was granted when it is a member of the role. Run it on the server that has the role.

CREATE ROLE zp_app_st LOGIN PASSWORD 'choose_a_password';
GRANT zp_st TO zp_app_st;

CREATE ROLE zp_app LOGIN PASSWORD 'choose_another_password';
GRANT zp TO zp_app;

6. In DMCR's first-run wizard

  • TEST connection postgresql://zp_dbo_st@localhost:5432/qs_test, schema zp_dbo_st, app role zp_st, password of zp_dbo_st
  • PROD connection postgresql://zp_dbo@localhost:5432/qs_prod, schema zp_dbo, app role zp, password of zp_dbo
  • Click Test on each, then set up each database in the wizard's last step. DMCR adds its dmcr registry there, owned by the admin user.

Change SQL names neither of them: CREATE TABLE xx (id int); and GRANT SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE ON xx TO ${app_role}; make zp_dbo_st.xx granted to zp_st on test, and zp_dbo.xx granted to zp on prod.

How one file becomes the right SQL on each

In the changeTESTPROD
CREATE TABLE xxzp_dbo_st.xxzp_dbo.xx
TO ${app_role}TO zp_stTO zp

The schema is each environment's Schema, used as its search path. ${app_role} is its App role. Both are in the first-run wizard and in Settings > DMCR Config.

If the SQL names one environment

  • The AI writes it: DMCR rewrites it before the self-check. zp_dbo_st.xx becomes xx, and TO zp_st becomes TO ${app_role}.
  • You type it on the card: Save to workspace refuses and says which file and name.
  • It reaches a deploy anyway: the deploy and its preview refuse with BLOCKED by environment names, on test and on prod.
  • An environment has no App role: a change using ${app_role} is refused there, and the message says to set it in DMCR Config.
  • Comments, ordinary strings and a table alias with the same name are not refused. A role with the same name on every environment can stay as it is.

Variables you can write in change SQL

VariableWhat it becomesSet in
${app_role}This environment's role: zp_st on test, zp on prodSettings > DMCR Config > App role
${your_name}Any value you add, the same on every environment. A ${name} with no value stops the deploy.[placeholders] in dmcr.cfg
__DMCR_CHANGE_ID__The change's idFilled in when you save

The Variables button in the top bar shows them with their values on each environment. Table names need no variable: write them with no schema.

What this does not check

  • DMCR only knows roles set as App role. A grant to any other role goes through as written.
  • A schema named on its own, as in GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA zp_dbo_st TO ${app_role}, is not refused, and it fails on prod. Grant schema access in steps 2 and 3, outside DMCR.
  • A change that names a role and is already applied on test needs its files fixed and running on test again before prod takes it.

The screens below were captured with schemas zp_st on test and zp on prod, connected as postgres. With this setup your screens show zp_dbo_st and zp_dbo there. The steps are the same.

When a sequence gives different ids on test and prod

DMCR deploys the same files to test and prod, and the promotion gate checks they are identical, so a change cannot carry a different id for prod. Each database generates its own id. Do not write the number in the SQL. Find the row by a column that is the same on both, such as a code or a name.

Find the row by its code

-- deploy.sql
INSERT INTO order_status (code, label)
VALUES ('HOLD', 'On hold');

-- child row: look up the parent's id on this database
INSERT INTO order_status_rule (status_id, rule)
SELECT id, 'notify'
FROM order_status
WHERE code = 'HOLD';

-- update by code, not WHERE id = 104
UPDATE order_status
SET label = 'Held'
WHERE code = 'HOLD';
-- revert.sql
DELETE FROM order_status_rule
WHERE status_id IN (SELECT id FROM order_status WHERE code = 'HOLD');

DELETE FROM order_status
WHERE code = 'HOLD';

What that did on each database

RowTESTPROD
order_status HOLDid 104id 57
order_status_rule.status_id10457

The next id was 101 on test and 57 on prod. Test ended on 104 because the round-trip test that runs before a deploy uses up numbers: a rollback does not give them back. Gaps like this are normal. After the revert on prod, the row and its child were gone and the other rows were untouched.

What goes wrong with a fixed id

SQL written from testOn prod
UPDATE ... WHERE id = 104Changes the wrong row, or no row, with no error.
DELETE ... WHERE id = 104The same, but it deletes the row.
INSERT ... (id) VALUES (104, ...), id takenThe deploy fails.
INSERT ... (id) VALUES (104, ...), id freeIt works, but the sequence does not move. A later insert fails when the sequence reaches 104.
INSERT ... (status_id) VALUES (104, ...)The child row points to the wrong parent, or fails the foreign key.

DMCR does not refuse these. The AI is told not to hard-code ids from one database, but no deploy check looks for them, so review any numeric id in a change yourself.

New rows with no such column

Keep each generated id in a backup table, so test and prod each revert their own rows. DMCR fills in __DMCR_CHANGE_ID__ when you save.

-- deploy.sql
CREATE TABLE dmcr.bak___DMCR_CHANGE_ID__ (id bigint);

WITH ins AS (
  INSERT INTO customer_note (note)
  VALUES ('first note')
  RETURNING id
)
INSERT INTO dmcr.bak___DMCR_CHANGE_ID__
SELECT id FROM ins;
-- revert.sql
DELETE FROM customer_note
WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM dmcr.bak___DMCR_CHANGE_ID__);

DROP TABLE dmcr.bak___DMCR_CHANGE_ID__;

For existing rows you need to change later, add a unique column such as code first, and give the rows already there their values.

If the id really must match

  • Do this only when another system depends on that exact number. Use a fixed id that neither sequence will reach.
  • Data Diff can move prod's sequence forward to match test. It does not write a change to move a sequence back, because those values may already be used.
  • Do not line up the sequences just to make ids match: rows already on prod keep their ids, so the lookup by code is still the safe way.

Before you start

Two DBAs, two DMCR Webs

  • anika.rao: DMCR Web on http://127.0.0.1:7821, her own clone of the repository
  • leo.martin: DMCR Web on http://127.0.0.1:7822, his own clone of the same repository
  • Open both in two browser tabs; the left edge of each step says whose tab it is

One release, two projects

  • A · Items (priya.nair): a table and two rows, for test only in this release
  • B · Pricing (marco.rossi): a function, for test and prod
  • B does not require A, so prod can take B alone

Every saved change

  • The card says Self-check passed (or Fixed before you saw it)
  • Project and Requested by on the card: a deploy is refused while a pending change has no project or no requested by
  • Save to workspace, then Commit: it pulls first, renumbers yours if the other DBA took the number, then pushes

Found and fixed during this run

Running these steps for real turned up these DMCR problems. Each was fixed and the whole run done again from empty; the screens show the fixed behaviour.

Fixed in DMCR

  • Two DBAs who changed the same function could deploy both: the later one silently replaced the earlier. A deploy (Releases and Runner, also its dry run) is now refused until a merge change resolves the conflict (c1377d9)
  • A deploy to prod listed the never-to-prod changes as NOT GOING, the word for a dropped change; it says NOT FOR PROD and 2 not for prod, skipped now, and the Releases deploy preview heads them 2 not for prod (581c808, ee8453d)
  • Both DBAs added the same function: the later revert dropped it, taking the earlier one too, so the merge change’s round trip was skipped. The revert now puts back the earlier definition and its verify accepts it (4094055, 372ca0b)
  • With both changes in one project the merge editor’s buttons read Accept B | Accept B; they say B · 003 and B · 004 now (4094055)
  • The 1 change saved but not committed banner stayed after a merge change committed; it refreshes at once now (155eb4a)
  • Releases’ auto-archive left releases.json uncommitted; it commits and pushes itself now. A deploy is refused, with a popup listing each change, while a pending change has no project or no requested by (5aaf7c8)
